# Direction Angle of a 2D Vector in Terms of Arctangent

## Statement

Let $\mathbf a$ be a vector quantity embedded in a Cartesian plane $P$, expressed in component form as
$$\mathbf a = x\,\mathbf i + y\,\mathbf j ,\qquad x,y\in\R,$$
where $(\mathbf i,\mathbf j)$ is the standard orthonormal basis of $P$. Let $\theta$ denote the direction of $\mathbf a$, measured from the positive direction of the $x$-axis (counterclockwise positive) and normalised to lie in the half-open interval $\hointl{-\pi}{\pi}$. Then
$$\theta=\begin{cases}
\arctan\dfrac yx & x>0\\[2pt]
\arctan\dfrac yx+\pi & x<0\ \text{and}\ y\ge 0\\[2pt]
\arctan\dfrac yx-\pi & x<0\ \text{and}\ y<0\\[2pt]
\dfrac\pi2 & x=0\ \text{and}\ y>0\\[2pt]
-\dfrac\pi2 & x=0\ \text{and}\ y<0\\[2pt]
\text{undefined} & x=0\ \text{and}\ y=0,
\end{cases}$$
where $\arctan:\R\to\openint{-\frac\pi2}{\frac\pi2}$ is the real arctangent.

The claim is **true**, and is proved below.

## 0. Conventions and the working characterisation of the direction

Write
$$r:=\size{\mathbf a}=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\ \ (\ge 0).$$

The direction of a vector quantity is the angle its representing ray makes with the positive $x$-axis. Analytically, this is expressed by the polar decomposition: $\theta$ is a direction of $\mathbf a$ if and only if
$$\mathbf a=r\left(\cos\theta\,\mathbf i+\sin\theta\,\mathbf j\right),
\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad
x=r\cos\theta,\quad y=r\sin\theta. \tag{$*$}$$
(Indeed, $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ is the unit vector making angle $\theta$ with the positive $x$-axis, and $\mathbf a$ is $r$ times the unit vector along $\mathbf a$.) The stated convention is that $\theta$ is taken in $\hointl{-\pi}{\pi}$.

Two things must therefore be checked before the case formula can even be discussed:

* if $\mathbf a\ne\mathbf 0$, equations $(*)$ have **exactly one** solution $\theta\in\hointl{-\pi}{\pi}$ (so "the" direction is well defined);
* if $\mathbf a=\mathbf 0$, then $r=0$ and $(*)$ holds for **every** $\theta$, so no angle is singled out and the direction is undefined.

The second point is immediate. The first is Lemma 1.

Throughout we use only the following standard properties of the real circular functions:
$\cos^2+\sin^2=1$; $\cos$ is a continuous strictly decreasing bijection $\closedint0\pi\to\closedint{-1}1$ (whose inverse is $\arccos$); $\cos t=1\iff t\in2\pi\Z$; the parity relations $\cos(-t)=\cos t$, $\sin(-t)=-\sin t$; the shift relations $\cos(t\pm\pi)=-\cos t$, $\sin(t\pm\pi)=-\sin t$; the addition formula for $\cos$; $\cos t>0$ for $t\in\openint{-\frac\pi2}{\frac\pi2}$ and $\sin t>0$ for $t\in\openint0\pi$; and the fact that $\tan=\frac{\sin}{\cos}$ restricted to $\openint{-\frac\pi2}{\frac\pi2}$ is a strictly increasing bijection onto $\R$, whose inverse is $\arctan$.

## 1. Existence and uniqueness of the direction

**Lemma 1.** Let $u,v\in\R$ with $u^2+v^2=1$. Then there is exactly one $\theta\in\hointl{-\pi}{\pi}$ with $\cos\theta=u$ and $\sin\theta=v$.

*Proof.* **Existence.** From $u^2\le u^2+v^2=1$ we get $u\in\closedint{-1}1$, so $\alpha:=\arccos u\in\closedint0\pi$ is defined and $\cos\alpha=u$. Since $\sin^2\alpha=1-u^2=v^2$ and $\sin\alpha\ge 0$ on $\closedint 0\pi$, we have $\sin\alpha=\size v$.

If $v\ge0$, put $\theta:=\alpha\in\closedint0\pi\subseteq\hointl{-\pi}\pi$; then $\cos\theta=u$ and $\sin\theta=\size v=v$.

If $v<0$, then $\sin\alpha=\size v>0$, so $\alpha\in\openint0\pi$ and $\theta:=-\alpha\in\openint{-\pi}0\subseteq\hointl{-\pi}\pi$; then $\cos\theta=\cos\alpha=u$ and $\sin\theta=-\sin\alpha=-\size v=v$.

**Uniqueness.** Suppose $\theta_1,\theta_2\in\hointl{-\pi}\pi$ both satisfy the two equations. By the cosine addition formula,
$$\cos(\theta_1-\theta_2)=\cos\theta_1\cos\theta_2+\sin\theta_1\sin\theta_2=u^2+v^2=1 .$$
Hence $\theta_1-\theta_2=2k\pi$ for some $k\in\Z$. But $\theta_1-\theta_2\in\openint{-2\pi}{2\pi}$, forcing $k=0$, i.e. $\theta_1=\theta_2$. $\blacksquare$

**Corollary 1.1.** If $\mathbf a\ne\mathbf 0$ then $r>0$, the pair $(u,v):=\left(\frac xr,\frac yr\right)$ satisfies $u^2+v^2=\frac{x^2+y^2}{r^2}=1$, and therefore there is a unique $\theta\in\hointl{-\pi}\pi$ with
$$\cos\theta=\frac xr,\qquad \sin\theta=\frac yr. \tag{$**$}$$
This $\theta$ is the direction of $\mathbf a$. Moreover, since $r>0$,
$$\operatorname{sign}(\cos\theta)=\operatorname{sign}(x),\qquad \operatorname{sign}(\sin\theta)=\operatorname{sign}(y). \tag{1}$$

## 2. Sign chart of $\cos$ and $\sin$ on $\hointl{-\pi}\pi$

**Lemma 2.** Let $\theta\in\hointl{-\pi}\pi$. Then:

| | |
|---|---|
| (a) | $\cos\theta>0\iff\theta\in\openint{-\frac\pi2}{\frac\pi2}$ |
| (b) | $\cos\theta=0\iff\theta\in\set{-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2}$ |
| (c) | $\cos\theta<0\iff\theta\in\openint{-\pi}{-\frac\pi2}\cup\hointl{\frac\pi2}{\pi}$ |
| (d) | $\sin\theta>0\iff\theta\in\openint0\pi$; $\ \sin\theta=0\iff\theta\in\set{0,\pi}$; $\ \sin\theta<0\iff\theta\in\openint{-\pi}0$ |

*Proof.* The three sets in (a), (b), (c) are pairwise disjoint and their union is $\hointl{-\pi}\pi$; likewise for the three sets in (d). Since "$>0$", "$=0$", "$<0$" are also mutually exclusive and exhaustive, it suffices in each group to prove the three implications "$\Leftarrow$"; the implications "$\Rightarrow$" then follow automatically.

(a) $\Leftarrow$: this is the standard positivity of $\cos$ on $\openint{-\frac\pi2}{\frac\pi2}$.

(b) $\Leftarrow$: $\cos\frac\pi2=0$ and $\cos\left(-\frac\pi2\right)=\cos\frac\pi2=0$.

(c) $\Leftarrow$: if $\theta\in\hointl{\frac\pi2}\pi$ with $\theta>\frac\pi2$, then $\theta-\pi\in\openint{-\frac\pi2}0\subset\openint{-\frac\pi2}{\frac\pi2}$, so $\cos(\theta-\pi)>0$ by (a), and $\cos\theta=-\cos(\theta-\pi)<0$. If $\theta\in\openint{-\pi}{-\frac\pi2}$, then $\theta+\pi\in\openint0{\frac\pi2}$, so $\cos(\theta+\pi)>0$ and $\cos\theta=-\cos(\theta+\pi)<0$.

(d) $\Leftarrow$: positivity of $\sin$ on $\openint0\pi$ is standard; $\sin0=0$ and $\sin\pi=-\sin 0=0$; and for $\theta\in\openint{-\pi}0$ we have $-\theta\in\openint0\pi$, so $\sin\theta=-\sin(-\theta)<0$. $\blacksquare$

## 3. Facts about $\tan$ and $\arctan$

**Lemma 3.** For $t\in\R$, $\arctan t$ is the *unique* $\varphi\in\openint{-\frac\pi2}{\frac\pi2}$ with $\tan\varphi=t$. Consequently, if $\varphi\in\openint{-\frac\pi2}{\frac\pi2}$ then $\varphi=\arctan(\tan\varphi)$.

*Proof.* Immediate from the fact that $\tan\restriction_{\openint{-\pi/2}{\pi/2}}$ is a bijection onto $\R$ (being strictly increasing and continuous with limits $\mp\infty$ at the endpoints) and $\arctan$ is by definition its inverse. $\blacksquare$

**Lemma 4 ($\pi$-periodicity of $\tan$).** If $\cos\theta\ne0$ then $\cos(\theta\pm\pi)=-\cos\theta\ne0$, $\sin(\theta\pm\pi)=-\sin\theta$, and hence
$$\tan(\theta\pm\pi)=\frac{-\sin\theta}{-\cos\theta}=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\tan\theta .$$

**Lemma 5 (sign of $\arctan$).** $\arctan$ is strictly increasing with $\arctan0=0$; hence $\arctan t>0\iff t>0$, $\arctan t=0\iff t=0$, $\arctan t<0\iff t<0$.

**Remark (why the case split must use the signs of $x$ and $y$, not the sign of $y/x$).**
When $x\ne0$, $(**)$ gives $\tan\theta=y/x$; but this equation alone does **not** determine $\theta$ in $\hointl{-\pi}\pi$. By Lemma 4, $\theta$ and $\theta\pm\pi$ have the same tangent, and $y/x$ is unchanged when $(x,y)$ is replaced by $(-x,-y)$ — a vector pointing in the *opposite* direction. So a rule that selects the branch according to the sign of the quotient $y/x$ is wrong (it cannot separate the first quadrant from the third, nor the second from the fourth). The correct extra information is the *pair of signs* of $x$ and $y$ separately, which by $(1)$ and Lemma 2 confines $\theta$ to an interval of length at most $\pi$ on which the tangent is injective. Every case below is therefore opened by locating $\theta$ from $(1)$ and Lemma 2 first, and only then inverting the tangent. Section 5 gives an independent verification of each branch that does not invert the tangent at all.

## 4. Proof of the theorem

The six cases
$$x>0;\quad x<0\wedge y\ge0;\quad x<0\wedge y<0;\quad x=0\wedge y>0;\quad x=0\wedge y<0;\quad x=0\wedge y=0$$
are mutually exclusive and exhaust $\R^2$. We treat each in turn.

### Case 6: $x=0$ and $y=0$

Then $\mathbf a=\mathbf 0$ and $r=0$, so $(*)$ reads $0=0,\,0=0$ and is satisfied by *every* $\theta$. No angle is distinguished, so $\mathbf a$ has no direction: $\theta$ is undefined, as claimed.

For the remaining five cases, $\mathbf a\ne\mathbf0$, so $r>0$ and, by Corollary 1.1, $\theta$ is the unique element of $\hointl{-\pi}\pi$ satisfying $(**)$.

### Case 1: $x>0$

By $(1)$, $\cos\theta=x/r>0$, so Lemma 2(a) gives
$$\theta\in\openint{-\tfrac\pi2}{\tfrac\pi2}.$$
Since $\cos\theta\ne0$,
$$\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\frac{y/r}{x/r}=\frac yx .$$
As $\theta$ lies in $\openint{-\frac\pi2}{\frac\pi2}$, Lemma 3 yields
$$\boxed{\ \theta=\arctan\frac yx\ }$$

### Case 2: $x<0$ and $y\ge0$

By $(1)$, $\cos\theta=x/r<0$ and $\sin\theta=y/r\ge0$. Lemma 2(c) gives
$$\theta\in\openint{-\pi}{-\tfrac\pi2}\cup\hointl{\tfrac\pi2}{\pi},$$
while Lemma 2(d) together with $\sin\theta\ge0$ excludes $\openint{-\pi}0$ and so gives $\theta\in\closedint0\pi$. Intersecting the two,
$$\theta\in\hointl{\tfrac\pi2}{\pi},\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \tfrac\pi2<\theta\le\pi.$$

Set $\varphi:=\theta-\pi$. Then
$$-\tfrac\pi2<\varphi\le0,\qquad\text{so}\qquad \varphi\in\openint{-\tfrac\pi2}{\tfrac\pi2}.$$
Since $\cos\theta\ne0$, Lemma 4 gives
$$\tan\varphi=\tan(\theta-\pi)=\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\frac{y/r}{x/r}=\frac yx .$$
By Lemma 3, $\varphi=\arctan\frac yx$, and therefore
$$\boxed{\ \theta=\varphi+\pi=\arctan\frac yx+\pi\ }$$

(Consistency: here $y\ge0>x$ gives $\frac yx\le0$, so by Lemma 5 $\arctan\frac yx\in\hointl{-\frac\pi2}0$ and $\theta\in\hointl{\frac\pi2}\pi\subseteq\hointl{-\pi}\pi$, as required by the convention. In particular for $y=0,\ x<0$ the formula returns $\theta=\pi$, which is the correct representative in $\hointl{-\pi}\pi$ of the direction of a vector along the negative $x$-axis; the value $-\pi$ is excluded by the convention, and this is exactly why the case $x<0$ is split at $y=0$ rather than, say, at $y>0$.)

### Case 3: $x<0$ and $y<0$

By $(1)$, $\cos\theta<0$ and $\sin\theta<0$. Lemma 2(c) restricts $\theta$ to $\openint{-\pi}{-\frac\pi2}\cup\hointl{\frac\pi2}{\pi}$ and Lemma 2(d) restricts it to $\openint{-\pi}0$. Intersecting,
$$\theta\in\openint{-\pi}{-\tfrac\pi2}.$$
Set $\varphi:=\theta+\pi$. Then
$$0<\varphi<\tfrac\pi2,\qquad\text{so}\qquad\varphi\in\openint{-\tfrac\pi2}{\tfrac\pi2},$$
and since $\cos\theta\ne0$, Lemma 4 gives $\tan\varphi=\tan\theta=\frac yx$. By Lemma 3, $\varphi=\arctan\frac yx$, hence
$$\boxed{\ \theta=\varphi-\pi=\arctan\frac yx-\pi\ }$$

(Consistency: $x<0$ and $y<0$ give $\frac yx>0$, so $\arctan\frac yx\in\openint0{\frac\pi2}$ by Lemma 5 and $\theta\in\openint{-\pi}{-\frac\pi2}\subseteq\hointl{-\pi}\pi$.)

### Case 4: $x=0$ and $y>0$

Here $\cos\theta=x/r=0$, so by Lemma 2(b) $\theta\in\set{-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2}$. Also $\sin\theta=y/r>0$, while $\sin\left(-\frac\pi2\right)=-1<0$. Hence $\theta\ne-\frac\pi2$ and
$$\boxed{\ \theta=\tfrac\pi2\ }$$
(consistently, $\sin\frac\pi2=1>0$, and indeed $r=\size y=y$, so $\cos\theta=0=x/r$ and $\sin\theta=1=y/r$).

### Case 5: $x=0$ and $y<0$

Again $\cos\theta=0$ forces $\theta\in\set{-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2}$, while $\sin\theta=y/r<0$ excludes $\theta=\frac\pi2$ (since $\sin\frac\pi2=1>0$). Hence
$$\boxed{\ \theta=-\tfrac\pi2\ }$$
(here $r=\size y=-y$, so $x/r=0=\cos\left(-\frac\pi2\right)$ and $y/r=-1=\sin\left(-\frac\pi2\right)$).

Since the six cases are exhaustive and mutually exclusive, the displayed formula for $\theta$ holds in all cases. $\blacksquare$

## 5. Independent verification of the three arctangent branches

The argument above *derived* the formula. It is worth verifying it in the opposite direction as well — i.e. checking directly that the proposed value satisfies $(**)$ and lies in $\hointl{-\pi}\pi$ — since by the uniqueness half of Lemma 1 this alone identifies it as the direction. This verification never inverts the tangent, so it is logically independent of the case analysis of Section 4.

Assume $x\ne0$ and put $t:=\dfrac yx$ and $\varphi:=\arctan t\in\openint{-\frac\pi2}{\frac\pi2}$, so $\tan\varphi=t$ and $\cos\varphi>0$ (Lemma 2(a)). From $1+\tan^2\varphi=\dfrac1{\cos^2\varphi}$ we get
$$\cos\varphi=\frac1{\sqrt{1+t^2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\frac{y^2}{x^2}}}=\frac{\size x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}=\frac{\size x}{r},
\qquad
\sin\varphi=\tan\varphi\cos\varphi=\frac yx\cdot\frac{\size x}{r} .$$

* **$x>0$:** then $\size x=x$, so $\cos\varphi=\dfrac xr$ and $\sin\varphi=\dfrac yx\cdot\dfrac xr=\dfrac yr$. Thus $\varphi\in\openint{-\frac\pi2}{\frac\pi2}\subseteq\hointl{-\pi}\pi$ satisfies $(**)$, so $\theta=\varphi=\arctan\frac yx$ by uniqueness.

* **$x<0$, $y\ge0$:** then $\size x=-x$, so $\cos\varphi=-\dfrac xr$ and $\sin\varphi=\dfrac yx\cdot\dfrac{-x}{r}=-\dfrac yr$. Put $\theta':=\varphi+\pi$. Then
 $$\cos\theta'=-\cos\varphi=\frac xr,\qquad \sin\theta'=-\sin\varphi=\frac yr,$$
 and since $t=\frac yx\le0$ we have $\varphi\in\hointl{-\frac\pi2}0$ (Lemma 5), hence $\theta'\in\hointl{\frac\pi2}\pi\subseteq\hointl{-\pi}\pi$. By uniqueness, $\theta=\theta'=\arctan\frac yx+\pi$.

* **$x<0$, $y<0$:** again $\cos\varphi=-\frac xr$, $\sin\varphi=-\frac yr$. Put $\theta'':=\varphi-\pi$; then $\cos\theta''=-\cos\varphi=\frac xr$ and $\sin\theta''=-\sin\varphi=\frac yr$. Since $t=\frac yx>0$ we have $\varphi\in\openint0{\frac\pi2}$, hence $\theta''\in\openint{-\pi}{-\frac\pi2}\subseteq\hointl{-\pi}\pi$. By uniqueness, $\theta=\theta''=\arctan\frac yx-\pi$.

Cases 4 and 5 were already verified in place. This completes the independent check. $\blacksquare$

## 6. Remarks

1. **The half-open interval matters.** The asymmetric treatment of $y\ge0$ versus $y<0$ when $x<0$ is forced by the convention $\theta\in\hointl{-\pi}\pi$. On the negative $x$-axis ($x<0$, $y=0$) the two candidates $\pm\pi$ represent the same direction, and the convention selects $+\pi$; the grouping $y\ge0$ with the $+\pi$ branch does precisely this. Had the normalising interval been $\hointr{-\pi}\pi$, the split would have to be $y>0$ versus $y\le0$.

2. **Continuity.** The function $(x,y)\mapsto\theta$ is continuous on $\R^2\setminus\set{(x,0):x\le0}$ but has a jump of $2\pi$ across the negative $x$-axis: for $x<0$, $\lim_{y\to0^+}\theta=\pi$ while $\lim_{y\to0^-}\theta=-\pi$. This is unavoidable for any single-valued direction function on $\R^2\setminus\set{\mathbf 0}$ with values in an interval of length $2\pi$, and reflects the fact that the punctured plane is not simply connected.

3. The function defined by the six cases is exactly the two-argument arctangent $\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)$ of computational practice.
